extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and designers studying Gothic and historical stone construction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for the form, proportion, structural function, and decoration of grouped (clustered) shafts and capitals in historic (especially Gothic) stone architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foiled (quatrefoil/trefoil/etc.) shaft family
rubrics_metrics.description: If the group at d3, Fig. XIV., be taken from under its loading, and have its centre filled up, it will become a quatrefoil; and it will represent, in their form of most frequent occurrence, a family of shafts, whose plans are foiled figures, trefoils, quatrefoils, cinquefoils, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These foiled plans occur frequently (examples cited from Venice and Salisbury). It is rare to find shafts of this family composed of a large number of foils because multifoiled shafts are seldom true grouped shafts but rather canaliculated conditions of massy piers. Treat multifoiled shafts cautiously — they often represent decorative or massive piers rather than true grouped shafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true grouped shafts from decorative multifoiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Some clustered shafts are little more than solid piers channelled on the surface; that clustering or striation is in this case a decorative feature, and to be considered under the head of decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume every ‘clustered’ appearance implies separate structural members — where the shaft is actually a solid pier with surface channeling, the clustering is decorative and must be judged as decoration, not structural grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concave-sided 'grouped' shafts as structurally weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts which have concave curves instead of convex on each of their sides ... are not, properly speaking, grouped shafts at all ... they have no representatives in good architecture, being evidently weak and meagre; approximations to them exist in late Gothic and modern cast-iron shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concave-sided profiles belong with decorated piers or specific classical types (Greek Doric) but are generally poor choices where genuine grouped-shaft function or strength is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not multiply shafts without visible structural cause
rubrics_metrics.description: he must never multiply shafts without visible cause in the disposition of members superimposed: and in his multiplied group he should, if possible, avoid a marked separation between the large central shaft and its satellites;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplication of shafts should be justified by the distribution of loads above. Excessive or gratuitous multiplication sacrifices structural honesty and can create visual faults (satellites appearing useless or as if wired to hold the central shaft). Examples of the fault given at Westminster Abbey and Bourges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marked separation between central shaft and satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: in his multiplied group he should, if possible, avoid a marked separation between the large central shaft and its satellites ; for if this exist, the satellites will either appear useless altogether, or else ... they will look as if they were meant to keep the central shaft together by wiring or caging it in ; like iron rods set round a supple cylinder, — a fatal fault ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing a clustered pier with a central dominant shaft, ensure satellites are integrated (visually and structurally) so they do not read as mere cages or trivial ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independent curvature only while shafts remain distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as they remain distinct and equal, however close to each other, the independent curvature may evidently be retained. But when once they come in contact, it is equally evident that a column, formed of shafts touching at the base and separate at the top, would appear as if in the very act of splitting asunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When grouped shafts touch, sacrifice tapering and adopt a true perpendicular line for the pier; execution must be done with greater accuracy and stability when members are delicately arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give grouped piers a true perpendicular line when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In grouping shafts, therefore, a true perpendicular line is, in nearly all cases, given to the pier;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly in closely arranged groups and those with a central shaft, straight/perpendicular piers are preferable because tapering would imply splitting; this requires higher accuracy in construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortness of minor members is required for serviceability
rubrics_metrics.description: the real serviceableness of any of these grouped arrangements must depend upon the relative shortness of the shafts, and that, when the whole pier is so lofty that its minor members become mere reeds or rods of stone, those minor members can no longer be charged with any considerable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grouped shafts where subsidiary members are short enough to carry loads; in very tall piers small satellites frequently become purely decorative and may be removable without structural consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using grouped piers simply to replace a single pillar for no reason
rubrics_metrics.description: the grouping of shafts once admitted, it is probable that the complexity and richness of such arrangements would recommend them to the eye, and induce their frequent, even their unnecessary introduction; so that weight which might have been borne by a single pillar, would be in preference supported by four or five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist aesthetic temptation to use grouped arrangements where a single pillar would suffice; consider material availability (stone beds) and structural economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure ring or joint stones correspond with wall string-courses
rubrics_metrics.description: to conceal the unsightly junction, a flat stone has been interposed, carved into certain mouldings, which have the appearance of a ring on the shaft. Now observe: the whole pier was the gathering of the whole wall, the base gathers into base, the veil into the shaft, and the string courses of the veil gather into these rings; and when this is clearly expressed, and the rings do indeed correspond with the string courses of the wall veil, they are perfectly admissible and even beautiful; but otherwise ... they are but sorry make-shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use rings/joints on shafts where they align with the building's string-courses and overall gathering — otherwise they appear as awkward make-shifts (similarly, beware of modern pipes that mimic rings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise three systemic families: Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: Egyptian system, an apparent cluster supporting a simple capital and single weight: Greek and Roman system, single shaft, single weight; Gothic system, divided shafts, divided weight: at first actually and simply divided, at last apparently and infinitely divided;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a shaft system that honestly represents load distribution: Egyptian (appearance of cluster but single weight), Classical single-shaft, or Gothic genuinely divided services. Understand symbolic and structural implications of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fusing shafts into nebulous aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: that all shafts of which we may have the ordering, shall be permitted ... to gather themselves into companies, or constellate themselves into clusters, but not to fuse themselves into mere masses of nebulous aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain legible order and definition in clustered shafts; excessive fusion into complex, ill-proportioned aggregates loses clarity and structural honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select capital root-form according to weight and function (a, b, c, e, g)
rubrics_metrics.description: a, though the germ and type of capitals, is itself (except under some peculiar conditions) both ugly and insecure; b is the first type of capitals which carry light weight; c, of capitals which carry excessive weight. ... the five forms ... are the roots of all good capitals existing, or capable of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplest forms as prototypes but choose among the root types (flat tile-like a; spurred b; filled c; truncated cone e; truncated pyramid g) according to the load to be carried and desired aesthetic; add spurs or fill crannies where support or weight-carrying is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abacus and bell as principal capital components and adapt their shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: The sloping stone is called the Bell of the capital, and that laid above it, the Abacus. The entire treatment of the capital depends simply on the manner in which this bell-stone is prepared for fitting the shaft below and the abacus above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the bell and abacus so they fit both shaft and abacus; different bell forms (conical vs pyramidal) require different truncation or cutting operations to fit the square/octagonal abacus or circular shaft and produce Norman, Lombardic, or Byzantine roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truncate bells by appropriate vertical/angle cutting to produce correct roots
rubrics_metrics.description: From the broad end of d chop or chisel off, in four vertical planes, as much as will leave its head an exact square ... which is the root of the greater number of Norman capitals. From / cut off the angles, beginning at the corners of the square and widening the truncation downwards ... this form ... is the root of nearly all Lombardic capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the described truncation methods (vertical planes on a cone to form Norman c; angle truncation on a pyramid to form Lombardic g) to derive classical capital families and to ensure fit between circular shafts and square/hexagonal abaci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dripstone (Early English) capitals for interior or load-bearing use
rubrics_metrics.description: The dripstone sections of their capitals ... are unnecessary and ridiculous. The edge of the dripstone, being undercut, has no bearing power, and the capital fails, therefore, in its own principal function ... the Early English capital has, therefore, the three greatest faults that any design can have: (1) it fails in its own proper purpose, that of support; (2) it is adapted to a purpose to which it can never be put, that of keeping off rain; (3) it cannot be decorated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject dripstone-profile capitals for internal or structural capitals — they undercut bearing, lack surface for decoration, and are misapplied to an indoor context.

rubrics_metrics.name: When shafts touch, accept loss of tapering and increase execution accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: But when once they come in contact, it is equally evident that a column, formed of shafts touching at the base and separate at the top, would appear as if in the very act of splitting asunder. Hence, in all the closely arranged groups, and especially those with a central shaft, the tapering is sacrificed; and with less cause for regret, because it was a provision against subsidence or distortion, which cannot now take place with the separate members of the group. Evidently, the work, if safe at all, must be executed with far greater accuracy and stability when its supports are so delicately arranged, than would be implied by such precaution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to give clustered piers a true perpendicular profile and higher workmanship precision when members touch; do not attempt tapering where contact would imply structural splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider proportional relations of shaft and capital as structural variables
rubrics_metrics.description: In this simplest condition, relations of proportion exist between five quantities ... These five quantities are: 1. The height of the shaft; 2. Its diameter; 3. The length of slope of bell; 4. The inclination of this slope ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must consider and possibly vary height, diameter, bell slope length, bell inclination, (and implied fifth quantity) to achieve correct structural and aesthetic proportion; proportions are a structural question, not merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure satellites are given 'work' and not merely ornamental
rubrics_metrics.description: in the most complicated Gothic arrangements, when the pier is tall and its satellites stand clear of it, no real work is given them to do, and they might all be removed without endangering the building. They are merely the expression of a great consistent system ... representing, for the sake of absolute consistency, the same bone in its appointed ... place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If satellites are introduced, either accept them as consistent symbolic elements or ensure they have an actual function; avoid adding useless satellites solely for ornament unless consciously behaving as symbolic consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regional/formal varieties with awareness of their climatic/origin functions
rubrics_metrics.description: the form of cornice which was gathered together to produce the capital was the root of cornices ... this was said ... to be especially characteristic of southern work, and that in northern and wet climates it took the form of a dripstone. Accordingly, in the northern climates, the dripstone gathered together forms a peculiar northern capital, commonly called the Early English ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that certain forms (e.g., dripstone capitals) originated from climatic needs; transplanting such forms into interiors or other climates can produce formal and functional absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ill-proportioned use of grouped shafts to create illusion of extreme slenderness
rubrics_metrics.description: The group is employed on a magnificent scale, but ill proportioned, for the main piers of the apse of the cathedral of Coutances, its purpose being to conceal one shaft behind the other, and make it appear to the spectator from the nave as if the apse were sustained by single shafts, of inordinate slenderness. The attempt is ill-judged, and the result unsatisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use grouping merely to create optical illusions of extreme slenderness if proportions are ill-judged; the device can produce unsatisfactory results when used to deceive the eye rather than express structural truth.
